the ai trade won’t bottom until market participants finally learn *not* to value companies based on fwd pe. 

a fwd pe of 40 is not necessarily expensive if earnings grow durably over decades. a fwd pe of 4 is not cheap if earnings last 18mo then go down 90%.

a company’s value is the net present value of *all* future cash flow, not the net present value of *next year’s* cash flow.

I'd like to believe LTAs are durable too. But take one example.

Analog chipmaker onsemi said this in 2023.
On January 5, 2023, at JPMorgan's CES forum, CEO Hassane El-Khoury was asked how much LTSAs would still hold once the shortage eased. His answer: “They are a legally binding agreement ’cause they’re a liability for the customer because they’re take or pay.” He also said he would not accept a customer reopening price talks just because it could get the same parts 10% cheaper elsewhere.

On October 30, 2023, on the Q3 earnings call, onsemi cut its SiC shipment forecast for the year from $1 billion to more than $800 million after one automotive OEM reduced demand. An analyst asked how this could happen when the company had been saying its LTSAs were legally binding. The same CEO reaffirmed that they were binding, but said he did not want to enforce the contracts just to push inventory onto a customer whose demand had dropped. If it worked for both sides, terms could be adjusted customer by customer, whether by a quarter, a year, or longer.

In its 10-K filings, onsemi also states that it amended LTSAs with some strategic customers by mutual agreement in 2024, and changed delivery schedules and committed volumes on some LTSAs in 2025 as demand shifted.

Microchip is another case. Customers in its Preferred Supply Program (PSP) originally had to place 12 months of orders and could not cancel or reschedule them unless Microchip raised prices. On its November 2025 earnings call, however, the CEO said the company had accepted some cancellations and pushouts so customers could adjust their backlog. On the same call, the CFO separately addressed the multiyear LTSAs the company had signed. Some of those contracts were still in effect, he said, but customers had been allowed to defer taking delivery of committed volumes by one to two years if they needed to.

Every time I see cases like these, I doubt how much memory makers' LTAs will protect earnings in a downcycle. Right now the most reliable thing is the prepayments and deposits themselves. That cash can go into capacity expansion today.

I can picture hyperscalers with no DRAM inventory continuing to buy at current prices. But once inventory has piled up, will they keep taking every committed unit at the same price? I have a hard time picturing memory makers holding customers to the high contract price all the way through.

The LTA itself may never be broken and may stay in place. But if both sides agree to push this year's volumes into next year or two years out, this year's earnings estimates come down. If price gets renegotiated too, margin estimates have to come down as well.

Again, I agree LTAs are sturdier than they used to be. What I question is whether, after demand turns, memory makers can still earn 80% margins on contracts signed during the upturn and keep collecting hundreds of billions of dollars in profit because of those LTAs.

PREDICTION MARKETS ARE TURNING OPINIONS INTO PARTICIPATION

People have always had opinions about what happens next. But prediction markets give those opinions a way to become active positions with measurable outcomes.

This is the space @sight_hood is exploring on Robinhood Chain.

SightHood is the first prediction market live on Robinhood Chain, with two different ways to participate.

The first is its short-duration UP or DOWN markets. Users can take positions on 5-minute, 15-minute or 1-hour rounds to participate in shorter market movements.

The second is categorical AMM markets, covering areas beyond price movements, including NFTs, stocks and other categories.

Here’s where things get interesting.

Market outcomes are settled transparently onchain, giving participants a way to verify how results are handled.

SightHood is also opening the door for creators through Creator Season 1. Participants create original content about SightHood and $SGT, earn points and compete for USDC and other rewards.

I look at prediction markets as more than a way to speculate. They create a structure where people express their views, take positions and see how those views compare with actual outcomes.

The real question is how well SightHood turns this participation into a sustainable market ecosystem.

That’s what I’ll be watching as the project grows.
